l: Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: This paper studies automatic distractor generation for multiple-choice questions, focusing on making incorrect options relevant, difficult, and useful. It develops two approaches: Retrieval Augmented Pretraining (RAP) and Knowledge Augmented Generation (KAG). RAP aligns pretraining with the downstream task by using an answer option to retrieve passages, masking the answer to form a pseudo question, and training a language model to generate the ground-truth distractors. It can use augmentation, cross-domain training, or ground-truth distractors during retrieval. KAG supplies a text-to-text generator with retrieved knowledge-graph triplets, selected using the question, answer, candidate distractors, and keywords, then ranked by sentence similarity or supervised classification. The work positions these methods against Generating-and-Ranking and Text2Text approaches, task-specific pretraining, and prior knowledge-graph use. It evaluates Text2Text, BART, T5, RAP, KAG, their combinations, and ChatGPT on SciQ, a 13,000-question science dataset, and MCQ, a cross-domain cloze-style dataset. Evaluation includes P@1, R@1, F1@3, MRR, NDCG@3, and human judgments of relevance, distractiveness, and utility. Results generally show gains from RAP and KAG. The best reported F1@3 rises from 14.80 to 16.47 on MCQ and from 15.92 to 16.50 on SciQ. However, combining RAP and KAG does not consistently add gains, potentially because triplets add noise and their ranker needs improvement. The paper also notes that token-based evaluation incompletely reflects output quality, while RAP may retrieve poor evidence for rare or specialized answers without a large knowledge corpus.

l: Distractor Generation, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Distractor Generation is an NLP task and research direction for producing distractors for multiple-choice questions, aiming to reduce educators’ manual creation time. It has two main research directions: a Generating and Ranking framework and Text2Text generation, with recent Text2Text work described as state of the art and Knowledge Graph integration relatively limited. The paper applies task-specific pretraining and knowledge augmentation to train or condition models for this downstream task. Evaluated on SciQ and MCQ datasets with F1, other automatic metrics, and human judgments of relevance, distractiveness, and utility, RAP, Knowledge Augmented Generation, and related methods improve generated distractor quality over baselines and reportedly outperform state-of-the-art results.

l: multiple-choice questions, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Multiple-choice questions are an assessment method widely used to evaluate learners’ knowledge. In the SciQ setting, each contains a question, one answer, and three incorrect options. The paper studies generating or selecting these distractors to improve incorrect-option generation.

l: Retrieval Augmented Pretraining, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Retrieval Augmented Pretraining (RAP) is a task-specific pretraining approach and data-augmentation design for distractor generation. It refines language-model pretraining by aligning it with the downstream Distractor Generation task and incorporating task-specific priors. RAP begins with MCQ options, using an answer or distractor as a starting point to retrieve a relevant sentence or short passage from an external, abundant corpus such as Wikipedia. It replaces the answer in the retrieved text with a mask token, producing a pseudo question. The pseudo question and ground-truth distractors then train a pre-trained language model to generate distractors during continuous pretraining, after which the model is fine-tuned for Distractor Generation. RAP can use the same dataset or separate datasets across domains. It improves distractor generation, with especially strong gains in some low-resource and cross-domain settings, and can outperform methods without RAP. Its retrieval may fail for rare or specialized answers, and combining it with knowledge graphs has potential for superior results.

l: language model, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: A language model is a pre-trained model that undergoes task-agnostic pretraining. It is used to generate distractor candidates through Generating and Ranking or Text2Text from a question stem and answer. In Retrieval Augmented Pretraining, it generates ground-truth distractors from masked retrieved text and an answer option, then supports triplet retrieval and supervised re-ranking.

l: Knowledge Graph, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Knowledge Graph is a structured knowledge representation that models entities as nodes and relationships as edges. It supplies structured background knowledge and triplets for inferencing, strengthening Natural Language Processing tasks, especially Question Answering and multihop reasoning, while complementing pre-trained language models in text generation. In this unit, it is explored chiefly to enhance distractor generation, an area with relatively limited application. Entities are extracted from the question, answer, and candidate set; graph triplets connecting keyword entities are retrieved, ranked, and added to the generation input in Knowledge Augmented Generation. This auxiliary information is intended to produce more relevant and challenging distractors. Finally, Knowledge Graph is identified as a component that, combined with retrieval augmented pretraining, may achieve superior results.

l: MCQ dataset, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: MCQ dataset is a cross-domain cloze-style dataset covering science, vocabulary, common sense, and trivia. It uses a shared 2321/258 train/test split, with training data further divided 9:1 for development. On it, the best-performing model raises F1@3 from 14.80 to 16.47.

l: SciQ, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: SciQ is a multi-domain multiple-choice question dataset of 13,000 science questions across physics, chemistry, biology, and other natural sciences. Each question has one answer and three incorrect options, with no blanks. Split 11,700/1,000/1,000 for train/dev/test, it supports distractor generation and cross-domain RAP pretraining; its best model raises F1@3 from 15.92 to 16.50.

l: F1@3 score, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: F1@3 score is an automatic metric for distractor generation, reported because test data contain three distractors. It is the harmonic mean of precision and recall at cutoff 3, where P@3 and R@3 are equal for label size three. Best-performing models reach 16.47 on MCQ and 16.50 on Sciq.

l: models, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Models using retrieval augmented pretraining and knowledge graphs significantly outperform state-of-the-art benchmarks, raising MCQ F1@3 from 14.80 to 16.47.

l: distractor, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Distractors are incorrect, non-answer options in multiple-choice or cloze questions. Designing them is described as the most challenging part of creating MCQs. They are generation targets in Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Augmented Generation, and are assessed for relevance, ability to divert from correct answers, and overall utility.

l: T5, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration

l: Text2Text generation architecture, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Text2Text generation architecture is a distractor generation architecture that frames distractor generation as a Text2Text task: it concatenates a question stem and answer and supplies them to a generative language model, including T5 or GPT. It is described as current state of the art. Evaluations with and without RAP and candidate augmentation show that RAP improves baselines on MCQ and SciQ and can outperform candidate augmentation alone.

l: task-specific pretraining, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Task-specific pretraining refines language-model pretraining to align with downstream tasks by integrating task-specific priors and using similar datasets. It improves low-resource fine-tuning, reduces overfitting, and can outperform masked language modeling when alignment is closer. The paper investigates it for distractor generation through Retrieval Augmented Pretraining, where integration with a knowledge base is associated with significant improvement.

l: multiple-choice question, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: A multiple-choice question training instance contains a question stem, an answer option, and distractors. Its answer and text are used in Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Augmented Generation. For task-specific pretraining, a sentence containing an MCQ answer is retrieved, the answer option is replaced with [Mask], and the resulting pseudo question is paired with the original distractors.

l: Knowledge Augmented Generation, Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
s: Knowledge Augmented Generation is a knowledge augmentation and candidate augmentation method for distractor generation, extended from prior work. It uses Knowledge Graphs as auxiliary tools to retrieve knowledge triplets, aiming to improve distractor relevance, create more challenging multiple-choice options, and improve use of structured knowledge. The method starts with keywords from the question, answer, and candidate set to retrieve relevant triplets, then re-ranks them to select triplets for generation. It augments a text-to-text generator’s input with the question, answer, and selected triplets, conditioning the model to generate distractors. It improves several baseline results, but its effectiveness depends on triplet selection: retrieved knowledge can introduce noise, and combining it with RAP did not consistently produce additive improvements. Its current design therefore has room to improve relevant-triplet selection.

l: R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: This paper introduces R2AG, an enhanced retrieval-augmented generation framework by Fuda Ye, Shuangyin Li, Yongqi Zhang, and Lei Chen. It addresses a semantic gap between retrievers, which rank external documents for a query, and large language models (LLMs), which must use those documents to generate answers. Standard RAG places retrieved documents with the query, while other enhanced approaches may add noise, cost, information loss, or require joint retriever–LLM training. R2AG is positioned as a cost-effective, non-destructive alternative, especially for low-resource settings where retrievers and LLMs are frozen. R2AG computes list-wise retrieval features from a query and its ranked documents, including relevance, precedent similarity, and neighbor similarity information. A trainable R2-Former transforms these features, and retrieval-aware prompting injects the resulting information into the LLM input embeddings. This retrieval information acts as an anchor for the LLM, helping it understand retrieved documents and reduce retriever–LLM miscommunication. The R2-Former is trained with both a query-document matching task and a language-modeling objective; the LLM may remain frozen or be trained. Experiments on Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and DuReader use accuracy, F1, and Rouge. Across frozen and fine-tuned settings and multiple LLMs, R2AG generally improves on its foundation LLMs and most enhanced RAG methods. Combining R2AG with RAFT produces the strongest overall results. Ablations and discussions attribute gains to retrieval features, query-document matching, retrieval-aware prompting, and stronger retrievers and LLMs. The paper reports robustness and efficiency, including only a 0.8% increase in inference latency. The paper notes limits: R2AG depends on encoder-based retriever representations; sparse and cross-encoder use is untested; performance depends on the foundation LLM and may not extend to more powerful closed-source LLMs; and other useful retrieval features may be absent. Evaluation assumes relevant documents are available, leaving no-relevant-document cases for future work, potentially with self-RAG. The authors state that public datasets and models were used, report no conflicts, and describe support from WT145-39, 2023A1515012073, and No. 62006083.

l: R2AG, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: R2AG is a novel, cost-effective enhanced RAG framework for retrieval-aware generation. It addresses the semantic gap between retrievers and LLMs by incorporating nuanced retrieval information into the LLM generation process without destructively altering the retriever or LLM. It begins with query and document representations from an encoder-based retriever, processes them into unified retrieval features, and uses a trainable R2-Former to capture retrieval information. Retrieval-aware prompting then supplies this information to the LLM, aiming to give it a more comprehensive understanding of retrieved documents. R2AG supports low-source settings: retrievers and LLMs can be frozen to save computational costs, with only R2-Former trained, though it also describes joint R2-Former and LLM alignment using query-document matching and language-modeling objectives. Across Natural Questions, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and DuReader, it generally improves foundation LLMs using standard RAG, outperforms most enhanced RAG methods, and outperforms ChatGPT on NQ and HotpotQA. It remains effective with long inputs, benefits from stronger retrievers, and achieves the best overall combined results with RAFT. Its limitations are dependence on encoder-based retriever representations, uncertain suitability for sparse and cross-encoder retrievers, possible incompatibility with more powerful closed-source LLMs, and difficulty when no relevant documents are available. Future work may add retrieval features or integrate self-RAG.

l: retrieval augmented generation (RAG), R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is a framework and method that augments large language models with external documents provided by retrievers. It retrieves documents useful to a query, binds them with the query through a predefined prompt template, and has an LLM generate an answer. RAG integrates external, non-parametric knowledge and gives LLMs flexible access to vast, up-to-date data, improving performance in domain-specific and knowledge-intensive tasks and extending to audio, images, and knowledge graphs through modality-specific retrievers. Its central limitations are sensitivity to retrieval results, increased complexity, and a semantic gap or miscommunication between retrievers and LLMs, especially when documents are noisy, numerous, or long. The unit introduces R2AG as an enhanced framework intended for this retrieval-and-generation setting.

l: retrieval information, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval information is the semantic representation supplied by retrievers in R2AG. It is transformed through an input-processing pipeline into retrieval-aware prompting, with R2-Former capturing nuanced retriever features. For each document, its unified features concatenate relevance, precedent similarity, and neighbor similarity scores, representing relationships between the query and documents and among documents. Integrated into LLM inputs, this information is intended to improve comprehension of key information and document relationships, fill a semantic gap, and aid generation. It serves as an anchor that guides the LLM toward useful documents: attention visualization shows retrieval information receiving higher attention in deeper layers, while the relevant document receives more attention in the first one to four layers.

l: large language models (LLMs), R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Large language models are generally decoder-architecture generators that answer questions from inherent knowledge or supplied documents. In retrieval augmented generation, they receive the original query and retrieved documents, process all results, and generate answers using those documents. Although trained on vast corpora, they can hallucinate, struggle with updated knowledge in knowledge-sensitive tasks, and produce incorrect or potentially harmful answers. They also do not fully understand why retrievers provide particular documents; differences between retriever and model objectives and architectures can cause incomprehension. Processing all retrieved material exposes them to noise, information overload, and the lost-in-the-middle problem, especially with overly long documents. R2AG addresses this by integrating retrieval information into generation inputs, including when models remain frozen, and can align its R2-Former with the model through language modeling. Experiments use open- and closed-source models as RAG baselines and foundation models; stronger models and more effective retrievers improve R2AG performance. The method ultimately provides documents and retrieval information to enhance generation and support a comprehensive understanding of retrieved documents.

l: retrievers, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Retrievers are typically encoder architectures that locate, gather, and rank the most relevant documents for a query. They encode queries and documents into semantic representations, supplying external documents and retrieval information to large language models. Their nuanced representations can distinguish differences among documents, but simple concatenation does not adequately communicate this information to LLMs, and their semantic spaces may be misaligned, creating a semantic gap. In the low-source scenarios targeted by R2AG, retrievers remain frozen. R2AG derives relevance, precedent-similarity, and neighbor-similarity features from their representations; stronger retrievers improve performance, while R2AG still improves LLM effectiveness when retrieval is poor.

l: semantic gap, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: The semantic gap is a misalignment between retrievers and large language models, caused by differences in their training objectives and architectures. It limits Retrieval Augmented Generation because retrieval and generation are often handled as separate processes. Existing preprocessing and compression methods generally do not resolve it, while joint modeling and latent-representation approaches can require extra training or be limited to encoder-decoder models. R2AG is proposed to bridge the gap: R2-Former and retrieval-aware prompting use retrieval information as an anchor during generation. From its identification as a mismatch, the records trace its limitations and alternatives to R2AG’s intended solution.

l: retrieved documents, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Retrieved documents are passed unidirectionally to large language models in RAG, usually in sequential or retriever preference order, but can include noise and low-quality material; long collections can obscure important information. Enhanced RAG methods use truncation, selection, evaluation, re-ranking, or compression. R2AG encodes each document and adds relevance, precedent-similarity, and neighbor-similarity retrieval-information embeddings to token embeddings. It is reported to help LLMs separate irrelevant documents, handle multiple documents, and use retrieval information during generation.

l: R2-Former, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: R2-Former is a lightweight, trainable, pluggable Transformer-based model in the R2AG pipeline between retrievers and LLMs. It bridges their semantic gap by mapping list-wise retrieval features into a higher-dimensional space, adding positional embeddings, encoding them with self-attention so unified features interact, and outputting essential retrieval information as additional embeddings for the LLM. It uses QDM loss.

l: retrieval-aware prompting, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-aware prompting is a method that injects retrieval information into LLM input embeddings and generation. It aligns retriever knowledge with LLMs without changing retrieved documents’ content or order, reducing information loss. It projects R2-Former information into token-embedding dimensions and prepends an anchor embedding to guide attention toward useful documents.

l: Enhanced RAG, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
s: Enhanced RAG is an enhanced approach based on the standard RAG framework that separates retrieval from generation while using the same foundation LLM. It improves retrieval through supervision, truncation, selection, evaluation, re-ranking, and compression, balancing reduced noise and complexity against inference costs or lost essential information; methods are frozen or fine-tuned.

l: retrieval information, R2AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation

l: PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: This is the front matter and full paper record for “PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers,” by Myeonghwa Lee, Seonho An, and Min-Soo Kim of KAIST, published in the Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1: Long Papers. The paper investigates LLM-based decision making over structured databases governed by business rules. It defines Decision QA: given a question, rules, and a relational or graph database, a model must choose the best decision. The authors create the DQA benchmark from 301 situations in Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3, yielding 301 question-database pairs and 602 databases. Its Locating scenario selects a trading node to maximize a country’s profit change, while Building selects a factory expansion to minimize a good’s current price. Savefiles are parsed into scenario-specific databases, questions are generated from templates, and simulators evaluate every candidate decision to annotate the best answer. The central method, PlanRAG, differs from ordinary RAG by having one language model iteratively make a data-analysis plan, execute SQL or Cypher retrieval queries, answer from results, and re-plan until no further analysis is needed. Experiments use GPT-4 with MySQL and Neo4j and compare Single-turn RAG, Iterative RAG, a no-re-planning variant, and PlanRAG. PlanRAG-LM obtains the highest accuracy, exceeding IterRAG-LM by 15.8% in Locating and 7.4% in Building. Planning and re-planning reduce missed analysis, candidate-selection, and retrieval errors, though reasoning and query-generation errors remain. Building prompts more re-planning because its database traversals are longer; adding look-ups is common in Locating, while splitting steps is common in Building. The paper contrasts DQA with prior structured-data and RAG benchmarks, which generally lack business rules and large databases. Additional model tests find GPT-3.5 works better with IterRAG-LM than PlanRAG-LM, while Llama 2 and Phi-2 solve no DQA problems. The authors note untested hybrid/vector databases, low-level query-generation improvements, and multi-model frameworks. They also warn that RAG does not eliminate hallucination or bias, anonymize nation names, and release the benchmark and simulator under the MIT license.

l: PlanRAG, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: PlanRAG is a proposed iterative plan-then-retrieval augmented generation methodology and RAG technique for Decision QA, designed for generative large language models as decision makers. Its central feature is that planning precedes retrieval: it examines the data schema and question to create a decision-making plan, then generates and poses queries to retrieve and analyze relevant data. A single language model carries out two types of reasoning: planning, and retrieving and answering. The process unfolds iteratively through planning, retrieving and answering, and re-planning. Retrieval continues until no further analysis is needed; if the plan, retrieved results, or initial plan are insufficient, PlanRAG re-plans and repeats the process before producing a decision answer. Experiments report that it outperforms compared RAG techniques and significantly outperforms SOTA iterative RAG on Decision QA, especially in the Locating scenario. It was implemented with a single LM, while effectiveness in a multiple-LM framework was not evaluated and is left for further study.

s: LLM is a model studied as a solution for decision making requiring complex data analysis and as a possible replacement for the human role in planning, data retrieval, and decision answering. It retrieves data from structured databases through data-analysis queries, but most RAG systems operate in a single-turn, non-iterative manner and were insufficient for this task. In PlanRAG, the language model performs planning and retrieval-based reasoning, generates plans, queries, answers, and re-planning decisions, and retrieves different nodes and edges by instance. Its use is limited by hallucination and potentially biased answers.

l: Decision QA, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Decision QA is a proposed decision-making task and benchmark for answering the best decision, dbest, for a decision-making question using business rules and a structured database. It requires more than answering: a language model must plan, retrieve data through data-analysis queries because the database may be too large for its input, analyze the retrieved data, select a best decision, and possibly re-plan. The task concerns complex questions that require considering both business rules and business situations represented in the database. It supports relational and graph databases; its RDB settings include Building with RDB, averaging 579.0 rows, and Locating with RDB, averaging 2038.8 rows, and every question requires access to all tables. PlanRAG addresses the task through planning, retrieval, answering, and possible re-planning. Experiments evaluate decision-making language models in zero-shot, single-run settings, treating an answer as correct when it is semantically identical to the ground-truth best decision. The study focuses on relational and graph databases, leaving hybrid databases, vector databases, and low-level solving methods for future research.

l: business rules R, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Business rules R are textual descriptions of formulas, data, and calculations used to reason about the best decision in Decision QA. They are one of three inputs, provided with a database and decision-making question, and are shared across instances. In the Locating scenario, they calculate trading power ratios, incoming value, and profit; in the Building scenario, total demand, total supply, and current price.

l: database D, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers

It may be a labeled property graph database or a relational database, representing business rules and business situations; in the example, it contains international trade, trading node, country, and related information used to calculate profit changes. D is queried during retrieval through data-analysis queries, executed in SQL or Cypher via RAG interfaces such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. Experiments use MySQL for relational databases and Neo4j for graph databases. D stores data extracted from each game's savefile according to each scenario's schema. Database instances can differ in row count and column values, including LV, building size, and current goods prices. As input to the Locating simulator and its three functions, D is updated with trading-power, flow, and IV values, then returned after profits are calculated. In general, it can be too large for language model input.

l: DQA, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: DQA is a benchmark for examining Decision QA, proposed because no existing benchmark can do so. It contains Locating and Building scenarios based on 301 specific situations from Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3. Each set includes a database, a question, and an answer or ground truth, with decision results deterministically calculated and recorded by developed game simulators as annotations. DQA uses business rules as language-model input, and prompt-structure experiments sample questions from each database setting. In experiments, Llama 2 and Phi-2 versions of IterRAG-LM and PlanRAG-LM cannot solve any problems in this setting.

l: Locating scenario, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Locating is a Decision QA benchmark scenario, constructed from Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3 as video game scenarios and represented in relational and graph databases. It uses data on countries, trade nodes, trading powers, values, flows, merchants, and directional source connections. Each eligible country has a problem, except countries with low TPcountry. In each instance, a different COUNTRY_NODE and HOME_NODE pair defines the goal: decide where to place a merchant so as to maximize the change in profit for the target country, including calculation of TPR to support the decision. The scenario contains a nation intended to influence a region, although nation names were anonymized as three-letter codes because correct influence recommendations could be aggressive. Locating is easier than Building because Building requires a longer traversal. It primarily uses Add look-up for re-planning. Reported results include PlanRAG-LM accuracy of 64.3% versus 48.5% for IterRAG-LM, with re-planning on 6% of questions; another reported Locating accuracy for PlanRAG-LM is 57.5%.

l: Building scenario, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Building is a Decision QA benchmark scenario constructed from Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3 as video-game scenarios. It uses relational and graph database representations and data on goods, buildings, supply, and demand. Each instance has a different GOODS value and asks which building ID to increase by five levels so that expanding factory production maximally decreases that good’s current market price. The scenario calculates current inputs, outputs, prices, and a TS value needed for the best decision; its goal is to minimize the current price of a given good. Problems with multiple answers are excluded. Building requires longer database traversals or more joins than Locating, making planning harder. In reported results, PlanRAG-LM achieved 45.0% accuracy and re-planned on 38% of questions, mainly by dividing into sub-steps; a prompt-structure comparison reported 50% accuracy. Table 11 reports GPT-3.5 results for IterRAG-LM and PlanRAG-LM on RDB and GDB. PlanRAG-based methods outperform the stated iterative RAG method by 7.4% in this scenario.

l: DQA benchmark, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: DQA is a Decision QA benchmark built from Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3 game data, using recorded decision results as annotations because real-world business data was difficult to use. It begins with two scenarios, Locating and Building, and contains 301 database-question pairs: 200 Locating and 101 Building. For each question it provides relational and graph database versions, totaling 602 databases, queried with SQL and Cypher Query Language. Nation names are anonymized as three-letter codes. Quality control omits low-impact countries and filters Building problems with multiple answers. It considers the EULA and is open-sourced under the MIT license.

l: RAG, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: RAG is a high-level technique and approach that augments language-model generation with external data. A retriever first finds data related to an input, such as a question, including results from database D through data-analysis queries; a language model then generates a response from the retrieved observations. Existing RAG-based methods mainly address knowledge-based question answering and make a decision through a single type of reasoning. In single-turn RAG, retrieval happens once; in iterative RAG, retrieval and generation occur multiple times. RAG can mitigate hallucination and biased answers to some extent, but these issues can still occur. In the reported experiments, it was not powerful enough to solve the decision-making task well, motivating high-level techniques for Decision QA rather than low-level RAG methods.

l: simulators for annotation, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Simulators for annotation are software developed for each DQA scenario. Constructed from Europa Universalis IV and Victoria 3, they use business rules to deterministically simulate every decision candidate: taking D with a decision, calculating its effects, and returning updated D. They concern gameplay and scripts of user generated content and are open-sourced under the MIT license.

l: planning, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Planning is PlanRAG’s central, traditionally human-handled step for determining the analyses needed for a decision. It takes a question, schema, and rules as input, generates an initial data-analysis plan, and guides retrieval. It unfolds by decomposing a decision question into steps such as identifying candidates, calculating potential profit changes, and selecting the best candidate; it is especially challenging for longer Building traversals.

l: retrieval, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Retrieval obtains necessary data by executing queries against database D for decision making and analysis. It may occur once in single-turn RAG or repeatedly in iterative RAG and PlanRAG, where results guide further reasoning, answers, or re-planning. Single-turn retrieval often fails on complex questions, while PlanRAG systematically organizes multiple retrievals.

l: decision answering, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Decision answering is the step in which a decision is made based on analyzed data. In PlanRAG, it follows planning and retrieval, unless the system determines that another plan and retrieval cycle is needed.

Different Building scenarios use GOODS when asking about decreasing market price.

l: ReAct, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: ReAct is a decision-making prompt structure that provides Thought-Action-Observation prompts, making LMs decision makers and underpinning previous RAG-based prompts, compared with planning-based alternatives.

l: re-planning, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: Re-planning is an event in which an insufficient initial plan is assessed against retrieval results and revised to continue analysis or correct earlier direction. It uses the question, schema, previous plan, and query results. Revisions may increase, preserve, or decrease steps through re-ordering, replacement, target changes, added look-up or calculation actions, division, deletion, or merging. It may occur repeatedly and belong to multiple categories. Removing it lowers accuracy, especially in Locating; it occurs more often in Building.

l: retrieving and answering, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: PlanRAG retrieves and answers by using a question, schema, rules, and initial plan to generate analysis queries; results drive iterative reasoning, re-planning or further retrieval, then a decision.

l: SingleRAG-LM, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: SingleRAG-LM is a single-turn RAG-based decision maker based on Single-turn RAG, implemented by GPT-4 with zero temperature and LangChain. It uses ReAct prompts for retrieval and answer generation, yet misses database results in over 60% Locating and 95% Building questions.

l: IterRAG-LM, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: IterRAG-LM is an iterative RAG-based language-model decision maker based on Iterative RAG. It uses a ReAct-style Thought-Action-Observation prompt and is implemented with GPT-4 at zero temperature using LangChain; results are also reported for GPT-3.5, Llama 2 (70B and 13B), and Phi-2. It reaches 48.5% accuracy in Locating and 37.6% in Building, with missed-data-analysis rates of 3.3% and 33.2%, respectively, and higher such rates than PlanRAG-LM. Its reported prompt-structure accuracy is 37.5% for Locating and 30% for Building. GPT-3.5 outperforms PlanRAG-LM, while Llama 2 and Phi-2 cannot solve DQA and score 0% in listed settings.

l: PlanRAG-LM, PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
s: PlanRAG-LM is a PlanRAG-based, RAG-based language-model decision maker implemented in a single-LM framework. It uses the Plan-Thought-Action-Observation-Re-plan prompt structure and conducts re-planning for questions; cases are categorized by step-count changes and plan-modification type, and a question can fall into several categories after more than two re-plans. With GPT-4 at zero temperature and LangChain, it achieved 64.3% accuracy in Locating and 45.0% in Building, outperforming IterRAG-LM by 15.8% and 7.4% and reducing missed-data analysis; its missed-data-analysis rates were 1.3% and 21.8%. In a prompt-structure comparison, it reached 57.5% in Locating and 50% in Building. Results also cover GPT-3.5, Llama 2, and Phi-2: GPT-3.5 performed poorly, while Llama 2 and Phi-2 could not solve DQA. Multiple-LM effectiveness remains unstudied.

l: BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: “BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation,” by David Rau, Hervé Déjean, Nadezhda Chirkova, Thibault Formal, Shuai Wang, Stéphane Clinchant, and Vassilina Nikoulina, presents an open-source Python framework and a systematic RAG benchmark study. RAG combines a ranking system, which indexes and retrieves passages for a user input, with a language model that generates an answer using the input and retrieved context. The paper frames RAG as a way to supplement static, potentially inaccurate LLM knowledge, while stressing that comparisons have been difficult because studies vary in datasets, collections, metrics, retrievers, rerankers, and models. BERGEN standardizes processing, indexing, retrieval, generation, training, and evaluation. It supports sparse, dense, decoder-based, and traditional retrievers; cross-encoder rerankers; open-weight LLMs; QA datasets; and training configurations. Its reproducible retrieval setting uses a fixed KILT Wikipedia collection of about 24.8 million 100-word passages. Answers can be evaluated with surface metrics, BEM, GPT-4, and LLMeval, which uses SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0 to judge whether generated and reference answers are equivalent. The study spans more than 500 experiments, including over 450 results across 10 datasets. It finds that LLMeval aligns most closely with GPT-4-as-a-judge and that semantic evaluation complements surface matching. Better retrieval generally improves generated answers, and reranking is particularly important; strong MTEB retrievers perform better in retrieval and generation, though reranking reduces differences between methods. Retrieval’s value is dataset-dependent: NQ is judged suitable because stronger retrieval and Oracle retrieval improve results, whereas closed-book performance exceeds retrieval settings on ELI5 and WoW. Retrieval evaluation uses Recall@5 mapped from KILT document annotations to the fixed passage split. The paper also finds that LLMs of any size can benefit from retrieval, while NQ QLoRa fine-tuning helps smaller models most and narrows their gap with larger ones. Multilingual experiments across 12 non-English languages use BGE-M3 retrieval, BGE-reranker-v2-m3, Command-R-35B, MKQA, and XOR-TyDi QA; multilingual Wikipedia retrieval is usually beneficial, but the best datastore depends on the dataset. The work closes by offering BERGEN’s modular framework, data, and runs while noting limits: computational constraints, one Wikipedia collection, mostly zero-shot QA evaluation, and limited scope beyond QA RAG.

l: BERGEN, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: BERGEN is an open-source Python benchmarking library and modular framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It standardizes easy, reproducible end-to-end RAG experiments and is intended to streamline the many configurations needed to train and evaluate RAG systems. Built on Hugging Face Hub and configured with Hydra, it covers data downloading and preprocessing, indexing, retrieval, reranking, generation, training, and evaluation; it also uses Pyserini for BM25 retrieval and vLLM for generation. BERGEN supports retrievers including BM25, SPLADE, CoCondenser, RetroMAE, BGE, RepLLaMA, and BGE-M3; reranking with Cross-Encoder, MiniLM, and DeBERTa-v3; and LLMs including Llama 2, Llama 3, SOLAR, Mixtral, Gemma, TinyLlama, and Upstage/SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0. It supports numerous evaluation datasets, analyzes existing RAG metrics and datasets, and enables full fine-tuning and QLoRA. Its study compares state-of-the-art retrievers, rerankers, LLMs, datasets, and metrics in question answering, described as the largest RAG study to the authors’ knowledge. BERGEN then extends to multilingual experimentation, using MKQA, XOR-TyDi QA, and Wikimedia Wikipedia, and presents a zero-shot multilingual RAG baseline across 12 non-English languages. Designed to be extendable, it provides data and runs for reproducibility, while planned additions include further retrieval models, LLMs, and datasets.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a knowledge-intensive NLP method and approach for addressing factuality challenges in Large Language Models by enhancing them with external knowledge. It retrieves relevant background documents or context segments from an external collection and explicitly provides them to a language model, enabling answers beyond the model’s internal knowledge. Formally, it consists of a ranking system R and a parametric generative language model θ, which use retrieved context c and user input x to produce response r; retrieval and reranking can provide top-5 passages to the LLM. Its central challenge is that results depend on a complex, multi-step pipeline: retrieval system, reranker, generator, dataset, collection, metric, and other design choices all matter. It therefore calls for unified, systematic training and evaluation. BERGEN standardizes experiments across retrieval, reranking, generation, training, and evaluation, supports varied architectures and resources, and emphasizes flexibility and extensibility through configuration files. Across hundreds of configurations, retrieval quality and dataset choice strongly shape outcomes. Improved retrieval, especially reranking, can substantially improve responses on suitable datasets such as KILT NQ, but retrieval may offer no benefit or reduce performance elsewhere; closed-book generation can outperform oracle retrieval on KILT ELI5 and KILT WoW. Evaluation uses retrieval performance, Match, and LLMEval across datasets, finding NQ suitable while ELI5 and WoW may be unsuitable for testing RAG. It is also evaluated on multilingual MKQA and XOR-TyDi QA, with improved multilingual performance across reported languages.

It generates a response from context segments and user input, and its knowledge can be accessed through prompting and question answering after alignment. This embedded knowledge is static, hard to inspect or update, and may be inaccurate or outdated. The records describe LLMs being enhanced with external knowledge through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and evaluated with retrieved documents or in closed-book settings. The records note that existing libraries and RAG studies use limited or inconsistent selections, while recent approaches may use outdated retrievers without refining rankings. The BERGEN study emphasizes state-of-the-art retrievers, especially rerankers. Retrieval systems are compared on KILT ranking-label datasets using R@5/Recall@5, with BM25, SPLADE-v3, RetroMAE, DRAGON+, E5, dense retrievers, and DeBERTa-v3 reranking. Their effectiveness in diverse out-of-domain contexts remains for further study.

The BERGEN study emphasizes state-of-the-art rerankers: DeBERTa-v3 reranking generally improves results, and retrieval quality strongly affects response generation.

s: Retrieval systems are ranking systems used to select passages and provide context for evaluating LLMs. Experiments compare BM25, RetroMAE, and SPLADE-v3 by retrieval effectiveness and downstream generation: higher-quality retrieval generally improves RAG, especially on NQ, but does not outperform Oracle on WoW and performs poorly versus Closed Book on ELI5 and WoW.

l: LLM-based evaluation, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a semantic evaluation [recommended beyond surface-matching metrics] LLM-based evaluation is presented as a form of semantic evaluation that should be used more extensively for RAG. It can assess answer quality beyond surface-matching metrics, which may fail to determine whether verbose zero-shot RAG answers are correct.

l: surface-matching metrics, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a evaluation metrics [commonly used but insufficient for semantic evaluation] Surface-matching metrics include exact match, F1, and Rouge-L. The unit states that these metrics can fail to capture correctness, especially when zero-shot RAG produces more verbose answers, and recommends supplementing them with semantic evaluation.

l: LLMeval, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: LLMeval is a simple LLM-based answer-equivalence evaluation metric in BERGEN for judging whether a generated response answers a question relative to a reference answer. It gives SOLAR-10.7B-Instruct-v1.0 a question, reference answer, candidate answer, and evaluation prompt in zero-shot evaluation, then converts its correctness judgment into a binary label; unexpected output tokens default to false. vLLM speeds inference, while extracted logits provide a continuous score comparable to directly generating one token. Reported alongside Match and used for SOLAR-10.7B on KILT NQ with retrievers and DeBERTa-v3 re-ranking, it is also used for multilingual RAG performance. Among tested metrics, it correlates most closely on average with GPT-4-as-a-judge and better overall with character 3-gram recall than other surface-based metrics, though that correlation is relatively low because it can assess valid answers across languages. It is recommended with Match and Recall for zero-shot RAG evaluation.

l: Natural Questions, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Natural Questions is a question-answering benchmark dataset with short reference labels, used for RAG evaluation and fine-tuning. Across experiments, stronger retrieval substantially improves performance, with Oracle retrieval achieving the highest performance.

l: TriviaQA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: TriviaQA is a large-scale, distantly supervised question answering challenge dataset for reading comprehension. It substantially benefits from added retrieval in zero-shot settings and has a 5.3k-example development split, where larger models generally achieve higher Match and LLMeval scores than TinyLlama-1.1B.

l: HotpotQA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: HotpotQA is a diverse, explainable multi-hop question answering dataset. Its 5.6k-example development set is evaluated with retrieval: retrieval notably helps in zero-shot settings, oracle context performs strongly, and SPLADE-v3+RR generally leads listed configurations in Match and LLMeval.

l: WoW, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: WoW is a dataset and knowledge-powered conversational dialogue task with medium reference labels. Across analyses, adding retrieved context worsens generation performance, and even Oracle retrieval does not help; closed-book systems outperform retrieval-based ones. Its 3k-example development evaluation shows near-zero Match values but substantial LLMeval variation by model and retrieval system.

l: ELI5, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: ELI5 is a long-form question answering dataset with long reference labels. On its 1.5k-example dev split, multiple language models and retrieval systems yield zero Match values while LLMeval varies. Retrieval performance is below 0.3 R@5, generation deteriorates with retrieved context, and Closed Book outperforms Oracle retrieval. Partial annotation or missing relevant documents may explain these results, making ELI5 likely unsuitable for RAG evaluation at present.

l: TruthfulQA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: TruthfulQA is a medium-reference language model evaluation benchmark measuring mimicry of human falsehoods; retrieved context reduces generation performance and offers no benefit, even with available oracle retrieval.

l: PopQA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: benefits_from retrieval [in zero-shot settings] PopQA is one of the datasets that benefits most from adding retrieval in zero-shot settings.

l: ASQA, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: ASQA is a question answering dataset combining factoid questions with long-form answers, and it gains substantial zero-shot performance from added retrieval.

l: BM25, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: BM25 is a lexical sparse retriever and baseline, achieving 0.531 retrieval recall on KILT NQ at R@5; it trails RetroMAE and SPLADE-v3, while reranking improves its reported performance.

l: SPLADE-v3, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: SPLADE-v3 is a learned sparse retriever and new information retrieval baseline. In experiments, it generally outperforms BM25 and RetroMAE on reported KILT retrieval results, reaches 0.799 recall on KILT NQ at R@5, and, with DeBERTa-v3 reranking, achieves the best overall performance and supports NQ fine-tuning.

l: DPR, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a dense passage retrieval method [for open-domain question answering] It is represented by work introducing dense passage retrieval for open-domain question answering.

l: DeBERTa-v3, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: DeBERTa-v3 is a cross-encoder reranker for additional ranking of retrieval results; it generally improves results, with SPLADE-v3 plus DeBERTa-v3 best among tested ranking systems.

l: Llama 2, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: is_a foundation and chat model [open] It is described as a family of open foundation and fine-tuned chat models.

l: Mixtral-8x7B, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Mixtral-8x7B is evaluated with oracle and closed-book generation, and its retrieval gain is smaller than those of several other models. Fine-tuning raises its LLMeval to 0.84, a gain of 0.05.

l: Wikipedia, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Wikipedia is a common source for providing external context to the LLM and the primary retrieval source in BERGEN’s collection setup. It supports fixed monolingual and multilingual datastore experiments, benefiting non-English queries. Its articles are divided into title-prepended 100-word passages, or 100 Unicode-character passages for Chinese, Japanese, and Thai, for retrieval across selected language collections.

l: OpenAI, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: It is the organization associated with the GPT-4 technical report and with earlier work on language models and instruction following.

l: BERGEN benchmark study, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: BERGEN benchmark study runs 500+ RAG experiments on retrievers, rerankers, and LLMs, concluding semantic metrics, quality retrieval, suitable benchmarks, and retrieval for all LLM sizes matter.

l: LangChain, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: LangChain is a RAG library and documentation resource, offering generic application modules for production-ready high-level RAG development and cited for language-model frameworks.

l: LlamaIndex, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: LlamaIndex is a RAG library and data framework for LLM applications. It provides generic off-the-shelf modules for production-ready, high-level RAG development, but offers limited retrievers, datasets, and metrics and lacks sufficient flexibility for research environments.

l: DSPy, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: DSPy is a programming-based, declarative language-model pipeline framework that creates compositional modules and compiles calls into self-improving pipelines, but lacks research flexibility.

l: RAGGED, BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: RAGGED is a RAG toolkit exploring optimal pipeline designs, including generation-model choices, but it lacks research flexibility and focuses on limited retrievers, datasets, and metrics.
